title: How many pieces is one word?
hook: You see one word. Does the model see one word too?

knows: that a language model reads text
doesNotKnow: that the text is cut into pieces from a fixed list before the model sees it
that rare strings cost more pieces than common ones

misconception: A model sees whole words, one per slot.
objective: The learner can explain that a tokenizer cuts text into pieces from its list, so common chunks cost one token and rare strings fall into many, and the model sees the pieces, not the word.

claims.text: With the pieces un, happi, ness plus single letters and longest-match-first, 'unhappiness' splits into un | happi | ness: 3 tokens.
With all three pieces switched off, 'unhappiness' becomes 11 single-letter tokens; 'zyxxy' matches no piece and becomes 5.
claims.source: tokenize('unhappiness', []) has length 11 and tokenize('zyxxy', PIECES) has length 5 in Demo.tsx (node).

claims.text: The three-piece vocabulary and the greedy longest-match rule are this toy's; they are labelled on the stage ('Toy tokenizer').
claims.source: Brief 31 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md. Real subword tokenizers differ in how they apply pieces (e.g. BPE applies learned merges in order).

claims.text: A model built on a tokenizer like this does not receive the word, only the row of piece numbers.
claims.source: About real systems: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch 2016, 'Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units', ACL (words are encoded as sequences of subword units); Kudo & Richardson 2018, 'SentencePiece', EMNLP demo (text to id sequence). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Opened the SentencePiece README (raw.githubusercontent.com/google/sentencepiece): a tokenizer 'for neural network-based text generation systems ... where the vocabulary size is fixed', which encodes raw text to vocabulary IDs (integers) and decodes IDs back; the model file holds the vocabulary mapping. Kudo & Richardson 2018 (EMNLP demos, D18-2012) and Sennrich et al. 2016 (ACL, P16-1162, pp. 1715-1725) not opened (arXiv/ACL Anthology unreachable); bibliographic details and the paper's 'NMT inputs and outputs are id sequences' corroborated by web search only. Suggest the builder add the README as a reachable source.

claims.text: Real tokenizers learn their piece lists from large amounts of text, so frequent chunks get their own pieces and rare strings fall into many.
claims.source: About real systems: Sennrich et al. 2016 (byte-pair encoding: repeatedly merge the most frequent symbol pair in the training text, so rare words split into more units); Kudo & Richardson 2018.

claims.text: A token is one piece of text that a model reads as a unit. The piece numbers under each box (#412, #7031, #1297, letters 1 to 26) are made up for this toy.
claims.source: Standard usage of the word token in language-model documentation; ids labelled on the stage as made-up.

claims.text: The stage keeps a record of the counts the learner has seen: 'unhappiness' (11 letters) costs 3 tokens with all pieces on and 11 with none; 'zyxxy' (5 letters) costs 5 because no piece fits it, so in this toy a chunk in the list costs one token and a string with no piece falls into single letters. In the reveal the stage returns to un | happi | ness.
claims.source: tokenize() and the record line in Demo.tsx: 'unhappiness'.length = 11, tokenize('unhappiness', PIECES) = 3, tokenize('unhappiness', []) = 11; 'zyxxy' contains none of un, happi, ness, so tokenize('zyxxy', any subset) = 5. The reveal quotes the 11 and the 5 only after the gate (both milestones) is reached. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node port of tokenize(): unhappiness length 11; all pieces 3 (un|happi|ness), none 11; zyxxy 5 under all 8 piece subsets. Record line in Demo.tsx adds 'no pieces: 11' and 'zyxxy, 5 letters: 5' only once seen; in phase reveal shownWord/shownTokens return to unhappiness with all pieces (un | happi | ness).

recall.question: A tokenizer has the pieces 'play' and 'ing' plus every single letter. Which costs a model more tokens?
options: They cost the same: one word each
recall.why: 'playing' is play | ing (2 tokens). 'qwzing' has no piece for qwz, so it is q | w | z | ing (4). The model sees pieces, and rare strings cost more of them.
